title: Cell Adventure 3 · Stretch
welcome_lead: Specialised cells, stem cells, and how one cell becomes two.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology stretch — specialised cells, embryonic vs adult stem cells, ethics, and the cell cycle (interphase, mitosis, cytokinesis).
final_note: You met specialised cells and their adaptations, compared embryonic and adult stem cells with their ethical issues, and walked through the cell cycle.

concepts.def: Cell with a shape suited to one job
Long tail, many mitochondria, packed with enzymes
Long thin extension — huge surface area for water
Unspecialised cell that can become other cell types
Nuclear division giving two identical daughter nuclei
Cytoplasm splits — one cell becomes two

walkthroughs.body_html:
Cells are shaped for their job. This is called specialisation.

- Sperm: tail to swim, lots of mitochondria for energy, acrosome enzymes to break into egg.
- Red blood cell: no nucleus (more room), biconcave shape, packed with haemoglobin.
- Nerve cell: long axon, branches at ends to connect.
- Muscle cell: long, lots of mitochondria, contains protein fibres.
- Root hair cell: long projection → huge surface area for absorbing water.

Stem cells are unspecialised — they can divide and turn into other cell types.

- Embryonic stem cells can become any cell type. Powerful, but using embryos raises ethical concerns.
- Adult stem cells (e.g. bone marrow) can only become a few types — used to treat leukaemia.
- Plant stem cells in meristems can clone whole plants.

Risks: rejection, viral infection from donor cells.

One cell becomes two in three big stages:

1. Interphase — cell grows, copies its DNA and organelles.
2. Mitosis — chromosomes line up and are pulled apart into two identical nuclei.
3. Cytokinesis — cytoplasm and membrane split into two daughter cells.

Result: two cells genetically identical to the parent.
